newsitem.title: USA: Commerce's Daley applauds greenhouse gas forum.
newsitem.headline: Commerce's Daley applauds greenhouse gas forum.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley Friday applauded international policy-makers and corporate executives gathered here for taking the first step toward a greenhouse gas emissions market.

The United Nations Conference on Trade Development and the Earth Council sponsored a policy forum in Chicago Thursday and Friday to begin the steps toward a world trading market for greenhouse gas emission by 2000.
Such a trading market was billed as a means to limit emissions and protect the environment from potentially far-reaching changes in the earth's climate.

"The move toward an international greenhouse gas emissions market, similar to the successful U.S. program for cost-effectively lowering acid rain, is both timely and appropriate," said Daley in remarks prepared for delivery to the Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading Policy Forum.

"We believe that the long-term threat of global climate change is real," Daley said. He noted that global surface temperature has increased and that the last few decades have been the warmest of the past century.
"The science is compelling," he said. "There is a discernible human influence on global climate."
The market approach to limiting greenhouse gas is to establish a cap on emissions in line with environmental goals, and then issue permits to companies to enable them to emit up to that capped level.
Companies that succeed in holding their emissions below the legislated cap are able to sell the spare capacity allowed by their permits to other companies looking for cost-effective solutions.
The policy forum is expected to meet again in October 1997 to agree on steps needed to establish the emissions trading system.
A similar system is already in place in the U.S. to limit acid rain.

Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) runs an annual auction for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency as part of a national acid rain control program. The CBOT auctions permits allowing companies to produce one ton of sufur dioxide. It is the first program of its kind in the U.S. to use market forces to curb air pollution.
